# WebsiteBench

> WebsiteBench asks whether AI agents can rebuild websites through browser exploration. Given a production-level website they can explore through a browser, agents must reverse-engineer a full-stack version that matches its appearance and behavior as closely as possible. It has 70 tasks with 46,916 hidden tests. Eight models were evaluated, each with a 16-hour time limit per run. The best overall score is 26.2% (Claude Opus 5.5).

## Benchmark
- A user workflow is a sequence of actions that completes a user goal and ends in an observable result, such as browsing products, adding an item to a cart, checking out and seeing an order confirmation.
- A URL path such as /cart identifies a route. The page at that route can show different states, such as an empty or full cart.
- An agent explores a locally hosted reference website through a browser: screenshots, interface state, navigation, clicks, typing and media downloads.
- It never sees the reference's HTML, JavaScript, CSS, API responses or server code.
- It builds a full-stack site that runs offline, within 16 hours, and may revisit the reference while coding and testing.
- Hidden tests then compare rebuild and reference. Request (T1) tests check page responses and form submissions. Browser (T2) tests check interface behavior at three levels: immediate responses (L1), state changes read back (L2), and persistence, other users and recovery (L3). System (T3) tests check builds, restarts, process health and security.
- A test scores 1 only if its functional checks pass and every visual checkpoint reaches the similarity threshold. Browser workflow tests repeat a sequence of user actions and check its result. Each must pass with two independent executors, Playwright and Browser Use.
- The Eval page compares one run with its reference: Qwen 3.8 Max on the Uber Eats task, which passes 39 of 338 hidden tests.

## Results
Table, Pareto and Waffle use the same results. Overall and Request/Browser/System scores are test-pooled: 100 × sum(passed tests) / sum(total tests). Cost, tokens and turns are per-task means.

## Leaderboard (test-pooled percent of hidden tests passed: overall / Request / Browser / System)
- Claude Opus 5.5: 26.2 / 71.2 / 21.8 / 35.4
- GPT 6.1 Sol: 20.2 / 64.3 / 16.9 / 36.8
- Claude Opus 5: 17.1 / 58.8 / 12.9 / 28.8
- GLM 5.3 Flash: 14.7 / 43.3 / 11.4 / 24.8
- DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: 13.5 / 39.9 / 9.8 / 29.7
- Grok 4.6: 12.1 / 39.3 / 8.3 / 29.5
- Kimi K3: 10.6 / 41.0 / 6.8 / 25.6
- Qwen 3.8 Max: 7.3 / 28.7 / 4.1 / 21.8

## Findings
- Underexploration: by their first code edit, agents had visited nearly every core page and started nearly every core workflow, but had followed only a few to their final result.
- A human exploration trace, a log of browser actions without page content, raised scores.
- Failure to implement observed behavior: almost none of the checked requirements that agents had observed were implemented the way the reference behaved. In an AMC Theatres run the agent opened /movies?tab=coming-soon, but its server ignores the tab query; in a PetSmart run the category cards keep their labels but show the wrong artwork.
- Early stopping: most runs ended well before the 16-hour limit. With Claude Code's /goal hook reviewing each attempt to stop, a Kimi K3 run on Lowe's continued from 1.0 to 10.9 hours and its score rose from 0% to 31.3%.

## Pages
- [Leaderboard and citation](https://website-bench.com/): Table, Pareto and Waffle views of the eight models, and the BibTeX entry
- [Run](https://website-bench.com/run): commands to run the benchmark with Harbor
- [Tasks](https://website-bench.com/tasks): the 70 websites, each with every model's result and screenshots
- [Eval](https://website-bench.com/eval): how a rebuild is evaluated, with one real run to compare
- [Analysis](https://website-bench.com/analysis): why agents fall short
